newsitem.title: USA: U.S. foreign crudes quiet, demand still soft.
newsitem.headline: U.S. foreign crudes quiet, demand still soft.

text.p: U.S. foreign crudes were subdued Monday on continued soft demand among Gulf Coast refiners, traders said.

A series of turnarounds and slim margins have suppressed refiners' appetite for crude. At the same time, an open transatlantic arbitrage has opened the door to North Sea and West African crudes, increasing the competition on the already crowded Gulf Coast, traders said.
The spread between benchmarks West Texas Intermediate and North Sea Brent for February was around $1.65-70 a barrel, down slightly from Friday but still wide open for transatlantic traffic.

The day featured plenty of talk if not actual deals, traders said. Brent for February 15-25 is on offer at February WTI minus 55 cents, although refiners aren't likely to take the crude for more than a discount of 70-75 cents, traders said.
Monday's most telling trade was for Colombia's Cusiana. An fob cargo for January 31 to February 1 traded at March WTI minus 60 cents.
The grade was last placed at a premium of 10 cents to March WTI for a January 23-24 cargo. Before the December holidays, Cusiana fetched a premium of 40 cents.

Incremental barrels, such as Ecuadoran Oriente, seem to be selling well. Key broker Tripetrol is sold out through mid-February. Oriente is selling for a discount of around $1.10 to West Texas Sour, traders said.
"Oriente is a good short-haul filler barrel," a trader said. The crude is also flourishing amid diminishing competition from Alaska North Slope crude.
In the U.S. aftermarket, a series of partial paper February Brent cargoes traded at $23.32/23.35/23.37 a barrel, 13-18 cents below the IPE settlement of $23.50.
Intermonth spreads were also weaker. Feb/March Brent changed hands at 35/37 cents, three to five cents below the London close.
